title: Stay at a hotel with a bed for your plushie in Japan
description: Complete with tiny matching pyjamas for your little friend. The world of fandom is vast and varied in Japan – on one hand you have fans who might show a casual interest in an actor, idol, VTuber, or anime character, and then on the other, you have diehard fans who engage in what’s known as […]
content:
Complete with tiny matching pyjamas for your little friend.

The world of fandom is vast and varied in Japan – on one hand you have fans who might show a casual interest in an actor, idol, VTuber, or anime character, and then on the other, you have diehard fans who engage in what’s known as “oshi-katsu”. Equivalent to the English slang term “stanning” – katsu means “activities” while oshi refers to the character or person you’re “stanning” – this level of fandom is reserved for those who go to great lengths to support the object of their affections at any given opportunity, investing time, effort and money into the activity, and treating it like a passionate pasttime.

One of the ways to show your love in the oshi-katsu world is by buying merch dedicated to your favourite idol or character, often in the form of a plushie, known as “nuigurumi” (“nui” for short) in Japanese. Nuigurumi are great for snuggling up to at night, and you can even take them out on trips with you, both near and far. It’s a passion that Japanese business hotel chain Toyoko Inn clearly understands, as it’s been officially catering to guests and their plushies since autumn 2025, when it started the “Oshi-Katsu Support Plan”.

A lot of fans would have stayed at Toyoko Inn for oshi events and concerts, so it’s a clever idea to create an accommodation plan geared towards them. There are actually two types of Oshi-Katsu Support Plans offered by Toyoko Inn – one is the “Relax & Recharge – Oshi Edition”, which comes with a free pack of foot care sheets, bath salts, and a heated eye mask to help you “unwind after a day of oshi-katsu”, while the other is the “Oshi-Katsu Sleepover Plan – Stay with Your Favorite Plushie!”, which gives you and your nui separate beds in the same room for the night.

▼ The stay is ideal for acrylic standees too, as this poster at the front desk reads: “We’ve started renting beds for plushies and acrylic stands.”

Our own reporter Maro, who has a few nuis of her own, was excited to try the Sleepover Plan, and when she learned that her plushie’s stay would cost a meagre 300 yen (US$1.88) on top of her room fee, she felt so heartened by the customer service that she packed several of her favourite plushies to join her on the sleepover.

Booking a stay for her and her plushie was a unique experience in itself, but when she got to the front desk, she was even more delighted when staff handed her a mesh bag at check-in, containing bedding and nightwear for her plush character.

While the stay is generally designed for one plushie, you could take several and let them share or rotate during your stay. The set contains a duvet, a pillow, a bed frame and nightwear in two sizes, though, so if you take more than two plushies, they won’t all be able to wear matching outfits.

As for where to put the bedding in your room, it fits perfectly into the curved space where you might normally put your smartphone and other small items when you go to sleep.

▼ The idea to repurpose this design feature into a toy bed is a work of genius.

Excited to give her nui the hotel experience, Maro took out the nightwear for her plushie. The nightwear gowns come in two sizes, small and large, and they have Velcro on the back, so they can be made to work with nuis, or standees, of various sizes.

Maro’s main nui has a rather large head, so the nightwear was bursting at the seams a little. The outfit would be more suitable for a regular human-shaped nui, but it still worked on her character plush, so it really does suit a wide variety of shapes and sizes.

Another cute feature is how the tiny nightwear matches the larger one designed to be used by human guests. Cue photos of you and your nui in matching nightwear during your hotel stay.

Though the nightwear required a bit of fiddling, due to the odd shape of her plushie, the bed slid into the space with ease. Within seconds, Maro had made the bed, and when she stood back to admire her work, she was impressed by how good it looked in the light.

▼ A tiny nook for your nui!

▼ Two nuis can fit in the bed if you rearrange their sleeping positions.

The space looked so good it was like it had been designed specifically for a nui bed, and the fun of the special accommodation plan doesn’t end there – if you post a photo or video of yourself using the plan on social media, you can also receive a “small gift”. Maro couldn’t find any information online about what the gift might entail, so she went ahead and snapped a photo of her nui looking as cosy as a bug in a rug.

[twitter https://twitter.com/hironamaro/status/2080639034653880681 align=”center”]

After sharing the photo on Twitter and showing it to staff at the front desk, Maro received…

▼… a toothbrush case set!

While the set doesn’t include a toothbrush – just the case and toothpaste – it’s an exclusive item that comes with a cute illustration on the front, making it as stylish as it is practical. She didn’t expect to get something so substantial in return for her social media post, so she was overjoyed by her free small gift.

▼ Her other plushie looked pretty happy about it too.

Looking into it further, Maro discovered that the toothbrush set is actually made from recycled plastic, sourced from used plastic toothbrushes and combs that are collected from Toyoko Inn hotels nationwide.

▼ Pop your used combs and toothbrushes in this receptacle in the bathroom, and you’ll be giving them a new life.

If you’re yet to discover the world of oshi-katsu, this type of customer service might seem a little mind-boggling, but for fans who go all out for their beloved characters and idols, it’s a dream service that makes for a very memorable stay. Even if you’re not into oshi-katsu, it’s a fun plan for guests with children who have plush toys that are like family members, and you’d be hard-pressed to find anything like it at any other hotel chain.

While no end date has been announced for the plan itself, the free-gift social media campaign runs until 31 August. So if you’ve ever dreamed of treating your plushie to a hotel experience that would make other plushies envious, now’s the time to book a getaway at the inn.

title: Japan’s Rabbit Island in danger of becoming Boar Island, tourists asked to follow feeding rules
description: One of the cutest places in Japan needs visitors’ help keeping rabbit food, and rabbits themselves, from becoming boar food. There’s an island in Japan’s Seto Inland Sea called Okunoshima. Written with the kanji 大久野島, Okunoshima’s name translates roughly to “Island with a Field from Long Ago,” which, to be honest, is a description you […]
content:
One of the cutest places in Japan needs visitors’ help keeping rabbit food, and rabbits themselves, from becoming boar food.

There’s an island in Japan’s Seto Inland Sea called Okunoshima. Written with the kanji 大久野島, Okunoshima’s name translates roughly to “Island with a Field from Long Ago,” which, to be honest, is a description you could apply to a lot of places in Japan. However, Okunoshima’s nickname is much more specifically descriptive: Rabbit Island.

Okunoshima has no permanent human residents, but the island is now home to more than 500 wild rabbits. Rabbits aren’t indigenous to the island, but were introduced to the environment sometime in the 1970s, with one theory being that the initial group was brought in by visiting children who’d raised the animals at their school and then set them loose on the island.

Regardless of how they got there, the Okunoshima bunnies got to doing what bunnies do, and the population grew to the point that pretty much as soon as you arrive in port, you’re going to spot wild rabbits who aren’t at all shy around human visitors. The little guys have no qualms about sauntering up to people in expectation of snacks, and many, if not most, visitors can be seen carrying around bags of chopped vegetables, either purchased from vendors on the island or brought from home, to feed the rabbits.

However, in recent years researchers have noticed some concerning changes in the ecosystem, and if not kept in check, there’s a risk of Rabbit Island turning into Wild Boar Island.

Like rabbits, boars aren’t native to Okunoshima, but researchers started noticing them on the island around 15 years ago, and have confirmed that they’ve bred on Okunoshima since then. The prevailing theory is that the boars swam over from the neighboring island of Omishima, based on reports from locals who say they witnessed such crossings.

▼ There is ferry service between Omishima and Okunoshima, but historically wild boars have been unable to surmount the challenges of navigating the reservation and payment systems.

Boars are not particularly picky eaters, and researchers believe that they’ve developed a habit of eating excess food that Okunoshima visitors leave for the rabbits. Basically, visitors, either because the bunnies are just so gosh darn cute or because they’re in a rush because they’ve got a ferry home to catch, have been putting out more food than the rabbits actually consume, but the boars are happy to chow down on the leftovers.

While this pattern is, technically, eliminating food waste, as a result of being well-fed the island’s boar population is increasing. This creates a risk of disrupting the ecological balance, and in recent years researchers from Fukushima University and the National Institute of Technology’s Kure College have confirmed cases of boars attacking rabbits on the island. There’s also the possibility that boars, which can exhibit aggressive or destructive behavior, could begin causing harm to human visitors or the island’s infrastructure.

Though attacks on rabbits appear to still be at an isolated-incident level of frequency, culling of boars via box traps is periodically carried out on Okunoshima. The preferable way for the situation to be handled, though, would be to not supply the boars with extra food to facilitate breeding. Since at least 2024, the joint committee created by the Ministry of Environment and the local tourism board have been asking that visitors who put out food wait and watch as the rabbits eat it. Should the rabbits not eat all of the food, visitors are asked to pick up any leftover portion to take home or otherwise dispose of in a proper garbage receptacle, so that it doesn’t become dinner for the boars. The committee is now once again calling for visitors to be conscious of the amount of food they set out and refrain from doing things such as dumping out the remnants of their bags in a pile before hopping on the ferry home, and hopefully travelers will comply so that the island doesn’t have to ban feeding the rabbits altogether.

Source: Yomiuri Shimbun, Ministry of the Environment

title: Time-lapse footage shows just how fast rebuilding in Kumamoto can go
description: All in a day’s work. Whenever major natural disasters hit Japan, I’m always amazed by the engineering feats that were set up in various places to minimize casualties and damage. It’s hard to feel a sense of joy or pride at times like the 7.1 magnitude earthquake that hit Kumamoto recently, but at the same […]
content:
All in a day’s work.

Whenever major natural disasters hit Japan, I’m always amazed by the engineering feats that were set up in various places to minimize casualties and damage. It’s hard to feel a sense of joy or pride at times like the 7.1 magnitude earthquake that hit Kumamoto recently, but at the same time it feels like a lot of hard work and ingenuity that goes into damage prevention often gets overlooked.

One prime example I noticed in the immediate aftermath was scenes of elevated highways sheared into two completely disjoined sections. It was constantly played on a loop as a symbol of the catastrophic power of the earthquake without any explanation as to why the roads looked like that.

▼ It was basically the exploded AEON Mall, broken smokestack, and broken highway, over and over again for the first day.

The highways were designed to break like that in the event of an earthquake to prevent even bigger devastation. If the entire overpass was one solid unit, one weakened section would cause the entire structure to fall down, as happened in the 1995 Awaji-Hanshin earthquake.

▼ A news report in the aftermath of the Hanshin-Awaji Earthquake showing the massive destruction of elevated expressways. In the latter part, Prof. Fukuwa explains that the flaw in the design was using combinations of materials that vibrated at different frequencies together in a rigid structure.

The news footage seldom, if ever, showed what was going on underneath those detached segments, which is where the real magic happens. Systems can vary as needed, but often these cables, rods, and stoppers not only reduce overall damage but make repairs easier and faster.

▼ This video is in Japanese, but the images alone should demonstrate how well-thought-out these mechanisms are, built on lessons learned from past disasters.

And speaking of fast repairs, with earthquakes an ever-present threat, crews are well-trained to react to damage quickly and thoroughly. A good example of this can be seen in a time-lapse video of a highway repair in Kumamoto done by workers for NEXCO, Japan’s privatized company that manages the nation’s expressways.

▼ “We are currently doing reconstruction work on the southbound/outbound lane of the Katanogawa Bridge along the Kyushu Expressway, after it was damaged in the 2026 Kumamoto Earthquake. This video shows the asphalt work in progress. The entire team is working in close coordination, prioritizing safety above all else. We will keep on working toward a fast recovery.”

令和８年熊本地震により損傷した九州自動車道　片野川橋（下り線）の復旧作業を行っております。
動画は、アスファルト舗装の実施状況です。
工事関係者が一丸となり、緊密に連携を図りながら、安全を最優先に工事に取り組んでおります。
引き続き、早期復旧に向けて着実に工事を進めてまいります。… pic.twitter.com/RnlYfZX9aU

— 【公式】NEXCO西日本 (@w_nexco_news) August 9, 2026

In the video, a stretch of collapsed and heavily crumpled road on the Katanogawa Bridge becomes a pristine sheet of asphalt in seconds, which in real time was about 10 hours, but still extremely efficient. Unfortunately, the speed also makes it hard to see all the work that goes into rebuilding the underlaying structure of the road in addition to repaving it.

It’s also worth noting that the date on the video is 8 August, the Saturday kicking off the national holiday period known as Obon, where a lot of people take off work and relax. That combined with the overall heat of a Japanese summer would make roadwork a particularly grueling experience. Comments online were full of respect for those workers, with wishes that they stay safe and get a fat paycheck at the end of all this.

“Seriously incredible! Thank you for your hard work in this intense heat and during the holidays.”
“They did that in 10 hours?!”
“That’s fantastic to see. Truly supporting the arteries of Japan, and you can sense the pride in their work.”
“I hope they’re all given big fat bonuses for that.”
“I used to work in asphalt, and I have a huge amount of respect for people who work under that heat and those tight safety conditions. I hope they stay safe.”
“It’s sad that politicians get paid more than those people.”
“I wish they could do normal road construction that fast.”
“But after doing it so fast, is it safe to use?”

I’m going to go out on a limb and say that if any corners were cut and safety regulations were ignored in this particular project, NEXCO wouldn’t post incriminating evidence of it for all the world to see online. Then again, I’m not a marketing expert. Maybe that’s the cool thing for companies to do on social media nowadays.

It’s just good to see things are getting better there bit by bit, and people’s ability to prepare for, prevent, and recover from disasters here remains something to be admired.

title: These Japanese contact lenses let you put anime characters on your eyes [Photos]
description: Chiikawa contacts are a cute way to add some subtle anime flair to your look. In Japanese, there’s a phrase, “Me ni irete mo itakunai,” which translates literally to “It won’t hurt even if you put it into your eye.” What could be so wonderous that you wouldn’t mind doing something ordinarily so painful? Why, […]
content:
Chiikawa contacts are a cute way to add some subtle anime flair to your look.

In Japanese, there’s a phrase, “Me ni irete mo itakunai,” which translates literally to “It won’t hurt even if you put it into your eye.” What could be so wonderous that you wouldn’t mind doing something ordinarily so painful? Why, something very, very cute, of course!

Me in irete mo itakunai is most commonly used by people to describe their children, grandchildren, or pets, but if we’re talking about cute things, we can’t forget about the anime/manga character Chiikawa, whose very name is a contraction of the words chiisai (“small”) and kawaii (“cute”). So today we’re going to be putting the compactly adorable Chiikawa into our eye…or at least onto it.

Allowing us to do this is En Giorno, a brand of contact lenses from Japanese cosmetics and merchandising company Shobido. En Giorno’s Chiikawa collaboration lineup consists of four models, Chiikawa Pink, Hachiware Greige, Usagi Brown, and Momonga Gray.

We opted to try out the Chiikawa Pink version, and naturally the character is featured on the packaging. There’s more to this crossover than that though, because Chiikawa is also on the contact lenses themselves!

Wasting no time, our Japanese-language reporter Natsuki Gojo promptly put Chiikawa onto her eye, and just like the saying had assured us, it didn’t hurt at all, though that probably has more to do with En Giorno’s precision manufacturing methods than the character’s cuteness.

Still, these lenses are indeed cute, and even more so than Natsuki had at first expected. It wasn’t until she had them in that she noticed that Chiikawa is surrounded by some illustrated sparkles, adding yet another dose of manga-aesthetic style to your eyes.

With the Chiikawa contacts in, Natsuki was looking forward to the excited reactions of friends and family throughout the day. Things didn’t unfold exactly as she’d expected them to, though, since no one, on their own, noticed her new ocular occupant.

This is, perhaps, something we should have seen coming. The En Giorno Chiikawa illustration really does follow the directives of both parts of the character’s name, as it’s very cute, but also very small.

▼ The Chiikawa contact lenses next to a Sylvanian Families baby plushie, the international scientific community’s widely accepted standard for scale comparisons.

On the other hand, every single person who Natsuki pointed out the Chiikawa illustrations instantly got a burst of giddy excitement from the revelation, and actually, the subtle size is probably a plus. For one thing, the illustration is compact enough that it doesn’t affect the wearer’s field of vision, and since it doesn’t immediately stand out, these lenses are pieces of Chiikawa flair that you can wear without disrupting your overall look.

▼ The En Giorno Chiikawa contact lenses come in both prescription and non-prescription versions, and are priced at 2,200 yen (US$14) a pair on the Shobido online store, Amazon, and Rakuten.

So while they’d be an apt choice for a meetup with fellow fans or when heading out to a Chiikawa event or anime screening, they’re also something you can use when just going about your daily life, so that if and when you do run into something unpleasant during the day, you can tell yourself “It’s OK, I’ve got Chiikawa with me.”

title: Japanese workers reveal their top five mysterious rules they wish would disappear【Survey】
description: A single vacation can lead to near-forced souvenirs and apologies to the entire office. Japan is world-renowned for its hospitality, respect for tradition, and attention to detail. In Japanese business culture, there’s also a dedication to politeness, where many customs were originally introduced to ensure smooth interactions and avoid conflict. However, as working styles modernize, […]
content:
A single vacation can lead to near-forced souvenirs and apologies to the entire office.

Japan is world-renowned for its hospitality, respect for tradition, and attention to detail. In Japanese business culture, there’s also a dedication to politeness, where many customs were originally introduced to ensure smooth interactions and avoid conflict. However, as working styles modernize, some of these thoughtful gestures have transformed into tiresome daily chores. To see which workplace rules have outlived their usefulness, Tokyo-based media company Mfro (via its Craudia crowdsourcing service) surveyed 493 working adults, 366 women and 127 men ranging from their 20s to 50s and older.

The top five mysterious workplace manners that Japanese employees secretly wish would disappear are:

5. Mandatory souvenir sharing (4.7 percent)

Bringing back local snacks (omiyage) for co-workers after a vacation or business trip is a way to share experiences and show gratitude, but when employees feel pressured to spend extra time and money hunting down treats, it becomes less of a thoughtful gift and more of a chore.

▼ “I heard you went to Okinawa. Where are the snacks?”

4. Excessive greetings (9.1 percent)

For anyone who has studied even just the basics of the language, you’ll know that polite greetings are the bedrock of Japanese communication. However, some offices take this to extreme levels that actually put a halt to productivity. These offices require staff to walk around the entire floor or department to greet every coworker individually upon arriving or leaving, or physically stand up at their desks whenever an executive enters the room.

3. Over-the-top chat messaging (11 percent)

Messaging apps like Slack, Line, and Teams are intended to speed up communication in the office, and yet traditional corporate etiquette has managed to sneak right into the group chats. Instead of quick, informal updates, workers feel forced to start every single message with long, formal greetings when sometimes a simple emoji reaction would wrap up the conversation effectively.

2. Vacation apologies and snacks (15.4 percent)

Paid leave is a legal right, but in a culture heavily focused on the collective team and the business instead of the individual, taking time off can leave workers feeling guilty about passing their workload to their teammates. Before taking a planned day off, employees might have to announce it to the entire office during morning meetings and, upon returning, they often feel obligated to go desk-to-desk apologizing for their absence and distributing snacks, even though they didn’t technically do anything wrong.

1. Rigid email etiquette (21.5 percent)

Japanese business emails are notoriously formal, requiring elaborate standard set phrases and seasonal blessings, and some offices even insist on listing all internal email recipients in strict order of corporate seniority, which feels like it’s wasting precious extra minutes that could be spent on real work.

▼ “Should I be using ‘intense heat season’ (酷暑の候, kokusho no ko) or ‘lingering heat season’ (残暑の候, zansho no ko) here?”

When asked about the biggest stress caused by these rules, 35.3 percent of respondents said it was “mental fatigue”, followed by taking up time (27.0 percent) and taking extra effort (26.6 percent).

Even if a significant portion of employees find the rules exhausting, it’s not as simple as just deciding to stop following them. The primary reason for not stopping was that they fear what others will think (36.1 percent), followed closely by the fact that it has already become the default norm (32.9 percent). In group-oriented work dynamics, stepping out of line risks making coworkers and your boss think you are rude or uncooperative. Among the respondents, some did mention that they had quit these mysterious manners, but are now looked at strangely by others at the office due to it.

So, these mysterious customs are more of a product of peer pressure and the traditional office environment, rather than being driven by pure logic. As remote work grows and generational turnover occurs, office atmospheres could potentially shift naturally, and these unwritten rules could slowly fade out of existence. However, to truly tackle these issues, the leadership needs to step in, recognize these problems, and create safe environments for employees to voice discomfort without the fear of social friction.

title: A practical guide to freezing your boss’ hat in a block of ice [Photos]
description: This is an important skill for working adults to acquire, and we’re here to walk you through the process step by step. Japan is in the middle of a very hot summer, and it’s got us scrambling to find new ways to keep cool. Earlier in the month we tried slapping 68 cooling patches on […]
content:
This is an important skill for working adults to acquire, and we’re here to walk you through the process step by step.

Japan is in the middle of a very hot summer, and it’s got us scrambling to find new ways to keep cool. Earlier in the month we tried slapping 68 cooling patches on the upper body of our crack reporter Mr. Sato, and while that did provide him with some measure of relief from the heat, we realize that such crazy methods may not be for everyone.

So today we’re going to be testing an alternate crazy method for staying cool this summer: freezing a hat.

Now that we’d decided on our plan, though, we had to answer the question of whose hat to freeze? After giving it some thought, we settled on swiping the hat of SoraNews24 owner and founder Yoshio off of his desk. The decision to give Yoshio this reprieve from the heat was made as a display of employee loyalty and appreciation for our boss’ hard work, and not at all because we weren’t sure if freezing a hat would ruin it and didn’t want to risk our own clothing in this experiment.

So how do you freeze a hat? First, you’re going to need a large bucket or similar container, like the cooking pot we grabbed from the office kitchenette.

Place your boss’ hat inside, upside-down, and stuff a plastic bag inside the hat.

Then fill the container with water…

…and stick it in the freezer.

▼ Eating any unclaimed mango ice cream that happens to be in the freezer is optional.

Exactly how long it’s going to take for the water to freeze will depend on your specific freezer setup, but we let our boss’ hat chill over the weekend, and when we checked on it three days later, that turned out to have been plenty of time.

After setting the pot out to thaw for a bit, we were able to pop the hat out, and it had frozen into a solid block shaped sort of like a curling stone.

Between the solid black color of the fabric and the texturing of the ice, it looked oddly beautiful, like a slab of high-quality polished granite.

However, we had a lot of work left to do before this ice hat would be wearable. Next we heated up some water and very carefully poured it into the plastic bag that we’d placed inside the hat. This melts the ice directly outside the bag without dissolving the other frozen area, clearing out space for the wearer’s head.

However, doing this means that the block of ice loses its uniform shape, and in the process the center of gravity is altered. In order to make this hat something that can be used without sliding off the wearer’s head, we’re going to need to grind off some of the excess ice using a straight file.

This isn’t a quick or easy task, and we felt our arms tiring before we were even close to finishing. Still, you’ll want to work carefully so that you don’t trim off any more ice than you need to.

Making things extra tricky is that while you’re shaving off the part you don’t want, the rest of the ice is going to start thawing. So rather than doing all the trimming and filing in one fell swoop, we needed to complete the process in stages. Once the ice we wanted to keep started seeming like it was in danger of beginning to melt, we put the hat back in the freezer to resolidify, then started filing again the next day.

On Day 2 we also expanded our tool set to include a heated cutter…

…and a heated soup ladle…

…respectively allowing us to make precise cuts or soften up a palm-sized area all at once.

Finally, on the third day of filing/trimming, we were done, and it was time to test whether our boss’ frozen hat would actually make him feel more comfortable.

▼ “Wait, didn’t I leave my hat right here?” asked Yoshio.

▼ Oh, do you mean this hat, boss?

Now, some of you might now be recalling the experiment we previously did in which we froze Yoshio’s glasses, and yes, we did that again this time.

Now reunited with his iced-over belongings, we invited Yoshio to try them out. He started with the hat…

…but when he completed his outfit by slipping on the glasses, the freezing sensation was shockingly intense!

Now, some might say that the proper thing to do here would have been to take these frozen items off. However, Yoshio is always telling us to look for outside-the-box solutions, so instead of removing the sources of pain-inducing cold, we moved Yoshio himself outside, where the chill could be offset by the scorch of direct sunlight.

We walked him to the park near SoraNews24 HQ, which, like a lot of downtown Tokyo’s parks, has some pretty extensive concrete paving which the heat reflects back off of.

Upon arrival, Yoshio could still feel the searingly icy sensation from his glasses’ frozen earpieces on his temples. By comparison, the cooling effects of the frozen hat were slower to manifest, but when they did, they brought on a strong chill at the back and top of his head.

But in time, things started to stabilize, and Yoshio, amazingly, reached a state of comfort.

▼ “Ah, this feels just right.”

▼ “From the neck up, it feels like autumn now.”

So while it’s a time-consuming process, yes, freezing your boss’ hat is an effective way to deal with summer heat. Of course, you could apply this idea to your own hat too, but that would mean missing out on one of the other benefits we were able to reap in our experiment.

Like we said, the cooling effect is so strong as to make the wearer feel uncomfortable in anything but the hottest environment. Should your boss remove his frozen hat while still in the office, though, he’s going to end up with water all over his desk as the ice melts.

So the best plan is to freeze your boss’ hat so that he’ll have to go outside, but won’t be able to come back in until the ice is melted. That way your boss gets to cool off, and you can get your boss out of your hair for a while as he stands thawing in the park.

title: Heavyweight ramen-style cheese fried chicken bowl appears in Tokyo, but is it genius or madness?
description: Karaage no Tensai invokes the name of Jiro-style ramen, and we head out for a taste test. It’s been said that there’s a fine line between genius and madness, but might that line be deep-fried and covered in cheese? It was the search for the answer to that question that recently led us to downtown […]
content:
Karaage no Tensai invokes the name of Jiro-style ramen, and we head out for a taste test.

It’s been said that there’s a fine line between genius and madness, but might that line be deep-fried and covered in cheese? It was the search for the answer to that question that recently led us to downtown Tokyo’s Uguisudani neighborhood.

We were here to visit the local branch of Karaage no Tensai, a restaurant chain whose name translates as “Genius of Fried Chicken.” Part of the Watami restaurant group (most famous for the Watami chain of pubs), Karaage no Tensai opened its first branch in 2018, so it was poised to reap the benefits of the boom in popularity for karaage/Japanese-style fried chicken that took place during the pandemic, when people across the country were looking for hearty comfort food that was takeout-friendly. By the middle of 2021, Karaage no Tensai boasted 100 branches, but these days the chain has dwindled back down to just six locations.

It’s kind of a shame, as Karaage no Tensai’s fried chicken (pictured above) is perfectly tasty stuff. Still, it’s hard to stand out when there’s so much competition in the karaage sphere, which is perhaps what led the Uguisudani branch to take the bold move of offering heavyweight ramen-style cheese karaage rice bowls.

Exclusive to the Uguisudani branch, Karaage no Tensai calls this creation the Jiro-kei Cheese Karaage-don, brazenly invoking the name of the style of ramen popularized by the Ramen Jiro chain, which has no connection to Karaage no Tensai or the Watami group. Jiro-style ramen, for those who haven’t tried it, is characterized by an extra salty and oily broth, copious amounts of garlic, and lots of bean sprouts.

▼ Ramen Jiro ramen

So how does Karaage no Tensai translate this into fried chicken form? Like this.

Visually, the 1,408-yen (US$8.85) Jiro-kei Cheese Karaage-don definitely makes an impact, with such a large quantity of toppings that they look like they’re about to overflow from the bowl and a surprisingly vivid cheese sauce squirted all across the top.

Starting from the bottom, the bowl is filled with rice, bean sprouts, six nicely sized pieces of karaage, cloves of roasted garlic, and cheese.

The cheese here is kind on an outlier, since it’s not an ingredient you’ll find in Jiro-style ramen. As our taste-testing reporter P.K. Sanjun took a bite, though, the reason for its inclusion became clear. The cheese sauce is strongly salty, and combined with its creaminess, seems to be Karaage no Tensai’s intended facsimile for Jiro-style ramen’s salty, oily broth.

However, the saltiness found in the cheese sauce isn’t present in the other ingredients in the Jiro-kei Cheese Karaage-don, and while the roasted garlic obviously tastes garlicky, P.K. couldn’t detect all that much seasoning to the bean sprouts of fried chicken. As such, salty cheese was the dominant flavor from start to finish, and the taste started to get a little repetitive part-way through the meal, prompting P.K. to munch on a mouthful of bean sprouts from time to time when he found himself wanting a palate cleanser or just a little variety.

All that said, the Jiro-kei Cheese Karaage-don wasn’t a bad meal. It may not actually scratch the Jiro-style ramen itch because of how different the fried chicken bowl ends up being, but it’s still a filling guilty pleasure of a rice bowl, even if it doesn’t really fulfil the promise in its name.

title: Kyoto shop turns traditional Japanese kimono into teddy bears, with special meaning hidden in their patterns
description: Mimirin in Gion gives us a new way to embrace Japanese culture… literally. Japanese kimono are an important part of the country’s cultural identity, but with changing lifestyles there are now less and less opportunities to wear them. This has led some people to come up with new and creative uses for kimono, to help […]
content:
Mimirin in Gion gives us a new way to embrace Japanese culture… literally.

Japanese kimono are an important part of the country’s cultural identity, but with changing lifestyles there are now less and less opportunities to wear them. This has led some people to come up with new and creative uses for kimono, to help keep the culture alive in the modern world, and one of those people is Mina Ichikawa, who came up with the brilliant idea to turn kimono into teddy bears.

Ichikawa, who studied Japanese culture at university in Japan and sustainability at Lund University in Sweden, first thought of the idea when her mother began working as a kimono dresser several years ago. After becoming aware of the huge number of kimono that were being discarded, despite the beautiful fabrics and traditional craftsmanship that went into making them, Ichikawa sought to find a way to repurpose them.

▼ She found her answer in the teddy bear – an object that transcends borders, appealing to people regardless of age or nationality.

Determined to make her dream a reality, Ichikawa worked hard on the designs, right down to the choice of fabric.

Through the use of auspicious motifs and patterns, she was able to imbue each teddy bear with symbolic meaning, making them even more personal and special.

After a successful crowdfunding campaign, which raised 550,050 yen (US$3,700), exceeding its 500,000-yen target, 24-year-old Ichikawa opened her first store, Mimirin, in Kyoto’s Gion district on 8 August.

With Mimirin’s slogan, “Bringing tradition into the palm of your hand” as its guiding principle, each Mimirin teddy bear is made using kimono fabric or an unused bolt of kimono cloth, and because the fabric is cut differently for every bear, no two are exactly alike.

Even bears made from the same kimono can look completely different depending on which part of the pattern is used and how the colours fall across the finished bear.

Combining beauty and symbolism, the bears make for meaningful gifts, and are perfect for souvenirs or special occasions like a birthday or new baby celebration. Some of the motifs you’ll find on the teddy bears are cherry blossoms, to represent new beginnings, asanoha (hemp leaf) for healthy growth and protection from evil, and chrysanthemums, which are traditionally connected with longevity and nobility.

▼ The bears start at 8,600 yen (US$53.98) for the small size, and go up to 18,000 yen for the medium and 26,000 yen for the large.

The shop also offers a custom-made service using customers’ own beloved kimono, so that rather than sitting unused in storage, a treasured garment filled with memories can be transformed into something meaningful that can remain with its owner for years to come.

By giving kimono a new life in the form of teddy bears, Mimirin hopes its products can carry the stories and wishes traditionally woven into kimono patterns into the future. The new shop in Gion, an area of Kyoto teeming with tradition, is said to be the first step towards achieving this goal, with plans to open more stores in tourist destinations around Japan and overseas in years to come.

title: Japanese convenience store sunglasses just became our newest Convenience Wear obsession
description: Family Mart has an “it’ll do” pair of sunglasses that might become your favourite pair. Sunglasses can be a bit of a hot-button topic amongst tourists visiting Japan, as they’re not commonly worn here due to their association with the yakuza. However, as Japan’s summers become increasingly hot and intense, attitudes towards sunglasses appear to […]
content:
Family Mart has an “it’ll do” pair of sunglasses that might become your favourite pair.

Sunglasses can be a bit of a hot-button topic amongst tourists visiting Japan, as they’re not commonly worn here due to their association with the yakuza. However, as Japan’s summers become increasingly hot and intense, attitudes towards sunglasses appear to be shifting. In the last couple of years, some prefectural police departments have started allowing officers to wear sunglasses while on outdoor duty (previously only officers on motorcycles and boats were encouraged to wear shades) and more and more stores are now selling them, including convenience store chain Family Mart.

Introduced this summer as part of the chain’s hugely popular Convenience Wear line, the new sunglasses retail for 2,490 yen (US$16.50), making them an affordable purchase when you’re out and in a pinch.

That’s what happened to our reporter Takashi Harada recently, who spotted the sunglasses at Family Mart on such a bright day that he decided right then and there that they would be worth the investment.

▼ The Family Mart sunglasses are unisex, with polarised lenses and UV protection.

▼ Most importantly, the lenses aren’t particularly dark.

In Japan, dark lenses are said to give off “iatsukan” (“intimidating presence”) vibes, which is one of the reasons they’re so stigmatised. That’s the reason why a lot of people who do wear sunglasses in Japan prefer lighter lenses that allow others to still see their eyes.

It was as if Family Mart knew exactly what would resonate with local customers, and although Takashi initially bought a pair as an “it’ll do” type of purchase, they ended up becoming his favourite pair.

As soon as he put them on, he was impressed by how well they fit. One of his pet gripes with glasses is how they can sometimes feel excessively tight on the temples and behind the ears, but these slid on like they’d been designed specifically for his face.

▼ The tiny Family Mart design details are another nice touch.

The lenses also suited him – although they have a Visible Light Transmittance of 30 percent, he had no complaints. Sure, they didn’t completely block the glare when the sun shone directly into his eyes, but they did a good job of reducing the sunlight for his purposes, which was taking a stroll outdoors.

▼ As long as you’re not staring straight into the sun, these do the job nicely.

What he liked most about the sunglasses, though, was how he didn’t have to worry about the way he handled them. He does own a pair of sunglasses that cost significantly more, but whenever he uses them he has to take a lot more care not to scratch them or drop them. At 2,490 yen, the Family Mart sunglasses aren’t quite as precious, so he now finds himself reaching for these a lot more often than he does his regular pair.

Family Mart actually sells two types of sunglasses – the Square style, which he purchased, and the Wellington style, which was released last year and has since sold a total of around 40,000 units. There are also brown lenses in addition to black, but they weren’t in stock at the store he visited, perhaps because of their popularity.

With shops like Uniqlo and Muji now selling sunglasses for less than 2,000 yen, Family Mart’s isn’t necessarily the cheapest option, but they do the job nicely, while looking stylish as well. Plus, there’s something special about being able to walk around with a pair of convenience store sunglasses on your face, elevating them from an “it’ll do” pair to what might just become your favourite sunglasses.

title: Tokyo giving out free furoshiki from Pikachu’s designer to help tourists carry their garbage home
description: The traditional, reusable cloth that can be converted into a bag is part of a new campaign designed to “Keep Tokyo Clean.” As we’ve covered before, public trash cans are a fairly rare sight throughout Japan. They were largely removed from public spaces following the 1995 Tokyo subway sarin gas attack as an added security […]
content:
The traditional, reusable cloth that can be converted into a bag is part of a new campaign designed to “Keep Tokyo Clean.”

As we’ve covered before, public trash cans are a fairly rare sight throughout Japan. They were largely removed from public spaces following the 1995 Tokyo subway sarin gas attack as an added security precaution since they would be an easy place to conceal explosives. Instead, Japanese people are taught to bring their trash home with them, a system that works well up till a certain point. Given the sharp rise in international tourists over the past few years, many of whom don’t know the system well or how to sort their trash appropriately, officials have noticed an uptick in the amount of littering happening, and consequently, some areas of Tokyo have implemented strict anti-littering fines this year.

As a further step to promote cleanliness, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government is in the process of rolling out a new Tokyo Clean-Up Action campaign with the catchphrase “Keep Tokyo Clean,” which is designed to spread awareness about the importance of not littering. Part of this campaign is the distribution of a furoshiki–Japan’s original eco-friendly piece of cloth–that can be easily converted into a bag used to carry your trash home with you while on the go.

▼ Furoshiki are a reusable piece of fabric, usually square in shape, that can be adapted for a variety of uses, including as wrapping cloths, bags, or decorations. They often feature traditional or fun patterns, such as these cat-themed ones found at Tokyo’s Nippori Station.

© SoraNews24

The Keep Tokyo Clean furoshiki are made from recycled polyester and feature images of Tokyo’s three AI-powered PR avatars the Tokyonauts, designed by artist Atsuko Nishida of Pikachu, Bulbasaur, Charmander, and Squirtle Pokémon design fame. Simply fold the furoshiki using the provided instructions to create a fun and handy bag in the face of your avatar of choice. The resulting bag’s size is big enough to fit a standard plastic drink bottle inside.

▼ The green owl-like character is Fukuhou, the red turtle-like character is Kikukame, and the yellow cat-like character is Tsutaneko.

If you want to get your hands on this practical and cute keepsake during your Japan trip, the Keep Tokyo Clean furoshiki will be available at various accommodations, lodgings, tourist information centers, and public events throughout Tokyo Prefecture for the next several months. It will similarly be up for grabs at a special kick-off event for the campaign on August 22 from 11 a.m. through 5 p.m. at the Omotesando Hills shopping complex in basement level 3’s Space O, where Tokyo governor Yuriko Koike will give a speech on the importance of maintaining a clean capital city.

For another method of keeping your space clean that leans on traditional craft, check out this old-school way of making trash containers from old papers.

title: Totoro shaved ice wows Studio Ghibli fans in Tokyo for a very limited time
description: Shirohige’s Cream Puff Factory turns the beloved Ghibli star into a very cool character. Shirohige’s Cream Puff Factory is known for its Totoro cream puffs, produced with the blessing of Studio Ghibli as director Hayao Miyazaki is a close relative of the owner. Though it now has two stores – one opened in Kichijoji, not […]
content:
Shirohige’s Cream Puff Factory turns the beloved Ghibli star into a very cool character.

Shirohige’s Cream Puff Factory is known for its Totoro cream puffs, produced with the blessing of Studio Ghibli as director Hayao Miyazaki is a close relative of the owner. Though it now has two stores – one opened in Kichijoji, not far from the Ghibli Museum, in 2019 – the one in Setagaya’s Daita neighbourhood has been the main location since it relocated there from Takaido in Tokyo’s Suginami Ward in 2013.

This is where a lot of new and creative limited-edition products are released, and now there’s an extra special treat coming to this location: Totoro no Yukidaruma, or “Snowman Totoro”. It’s become something of an annual summer tradition for these sorts of Totoro shaved ice desserts to appear at the store, with the icy Totoros appearing last year and the year before, but this year things look very different, because unlike previous years, the shaved ice is shaped to look like Totoro.

There are three flavours in this year’s lineup, with each one containing a scoop of ice cream, some cubes of kanten (agar agar jelly), and a special “Mini Totoro” made using the same traditional nerikiri technique used to create moulded wagashi sweets.

▼ The sweet little Totoro is designed to sit on a mint leaf atop each Totoro.

▼ The first flavour in the Totoro trifecta is Strawberry.

Bright red fruit brings colour and a burst of flavour to this Totoro, with a sauce made with “Sachinoka” strawberries from Nagano Prefecture. Containing nothing but strawberries and sugar in the sauce, which has been left pulpy so you can enjoy the sweet tartness of the fruit, this unfettered dessert keeps things simple with fresh strawberries and a scoop of vanilla ice cream.

▼ Peach

This variety is said to be the most popular with staff at the store, and it’s easy to see why. Not only does it contain thick slices of domestically produced white peaches, it also includes a special sauce made from nectarines and plums that have been slowly simmered and carefully strained. Finished with fresh, sweet white peach syrup, the sauce showcases the gentle sweetness of white peaches, and is complemented by the refreshing flavour of nectarines and plums, creating a perfectly balanced sweet and tart taste.

▼ Matcha

Green tea lovers will go weak at the knees for this Totoro, which contains matcha ice cream and matcha syrup made with a generous amount of fragrant Uji matcha. By adding anko red bean paste, shiratama dumplings and kanten (in this case both plain and matcha kanten), this dessert is evocative of a popular traditional Japanese dessert called anmitsu, which contains all three of these ingredients. The addition of milk and fresh cream, and white chocolate as a “secret” ingredient, helps to round out the matcha-centric flavours, adding just the right amount of sweetness to complement the satisfying bitterness of the matcha.

Priced at 2,000 yen (US$12.55) each, the Snowman Totoros will be sold from 10:30 a.m. on six days only: 21-23 August and 28-30 August. As the Totoros can’t be taken home they have to be eaten on the premises, and in order to keep things moving along smoothly, customers are being asked to wait until all members of their party are present before joining the queue. They explicitly ask that people refrain from having one person line up first and then have their companions join them later, as the store is small and the queue is expected to be long, and Shirohige’s wants as many people as possible to enjoy the shaved ice. Supplies are limited, though, so you’ll want to get there early and gobble your Totoro quickly, so everyone lining up in the heat can get a cool taste of Totoro.

title: Starbucks Japan releases two new seasonal drinks that blur the line between summer and autumn
description: We find out if Starbucks does justice to a fruit with a very Japanese flavour.  As we make our way through August, we’re now beginning to see signs of autumn approaching, with earlier sunsets, the sounds of insects in the evening, and… new seasonal beverages at Starbucks. This year, Japan’s prized Kyoho grape variety is […]
content:
We find out if Starbucks does justice to a fruit with a very Japanese flavour. 

As we make our way through August, we’re now beginning to see signs of autumn approaching, with earlier sunsets, the sounds of insects in the evening, and… new seasonal beverages at Starbucks.

This year, Japan’s prized Kyoho grape variety is the harbinger of autumn at Starbucks, with not one but two new drinks featuring the autumnal fruit, with a cold and icy twist to keep us refreshed while the weather remains warm.

Our resident Starbucks expert K. Masami headed out to try the new drinks when they were released on 17 August, starting first with the “Rich Kyoho Frozen Tea” (680 yen (US$4.27).

This icy beverage lets the fruit shine, with the help of black tea and cassis, the latter of which is added as a “hidden component” to enhance the flavour. Towards the base of the glass, you’ll find a very generous mound of Kyoho jelly and fruit pulp, which greets the palate upon first sip with mouthfuls of fruity refreshment. Masami loved the way the pulp and jelly helped to dial down the astringency off the straight black tea, reducing its bitterness while giving it a clean finish that made it very easy to drink. The flavour and mouthfeel of the base added a sense of sweetness, juciness and richness to the beverage, and although Masami had an inkling that grape and tea would pair well together, she had no idea they would taste this good. Kyoho is a quintessential Japanese flavour, and this tea really allows that taste to be front and centre on the palate.

▼ How would the Chillax Soda compare?

On the menu from 590 yen, the Kyoho Chillax Soda is slightly cheaper than the tea, but as soon as Masami took a sip, she realised it was no less delicious. Chillax sodas, which contain a special “green citrus” syrup, have become very popular since they were first released in 2025, and this new grape variety pairs surprisingly well with the lemony lime hints in the carbonated beverage. In trying to describe the flavour, Masami says it’s as if you’ve popped a slightly wild-tasting Kyoho grape in your mouth, giving you a burst of energy that acts like a reset for your mind and body.

Both drinks were so good that in the end, Masami wasn’t able to pick a favourite. They both deliver a delicious Japanese grape flavour, and are great for perking yourself up on a late summer’s day. The only thing is that, like always, these seasonal beverages are only available for a limited time, so you’ll want to get in quick to try them before they disappear from the menu.

title: Dog-friendly Wanwan Liner bus to begin operations between Tokyo and Osaka this fall
description: This upcoming doggy express offers a new option for long-distance travel in comfort with your Best Friend. For many, the worst part of traveling long distance has nothing to do with the journey itself, but the sadness of leaving your beloved furry friends behind. Though JR East has experimented with limited-time dog-friendly options before, it’s […]
content:
This upcoming doggy express offers a new option for long-distance travel in comfort with your Best Friend.

For many, the worst part of traveling long distance has nothing to do with the journey itself, but the sadness of leaving your beloved furry friends behind. Though JR East has experimented with limited-time dog-friendly options before, it’s always been wishful thinking that there could be a consistently easy way for them to ride alongside you on public transportation…but now, that wish is about to become an actual reality.

Tokyo-based transportation company B・I・G Bus has announced that it plans to begin operating a new Wanwan Liner (“Woof-woof Liner”) bus service between Tokyo and Osaka on November 1, pending approval of all necessary agencies. The company is no stranger to dog-friendly travel, already offering over 100 such plans, but this newest initiative is meant to provide a practical way to travel with your dog in a secure, stress-free environment between two of Japan’s largest cities.

▼ The Wanwan Liner, complete with cute pawprints on its exterior

Dog owners may already be wondering what the eligibility criteria are for their precious pups to ride on the bus, but specific details have yet to be announced. However, the company has confirmed that there will be strict rules for riding, safety checks, as well as sanitation and odor-prevention measures enacted to ensure your peace of mind throughout the journey.

Furthermore, Wanwan Liner buses will schedule longer-than-usual stops at rest areas and service locations so that doggos will have extra time to use the facilities’ attached dog runs to stretch and get a little exercise in mid-trip.

▼ Partitions can apparently be put in place to help keep pets near their owners while onboard the bus.

Even though details on the Wanwan Liner are still sparse, this announcement could be that push that you need to book your next stay in either Tokyo or Osaka with your furry friend. We only hope that hotels will become more accommodating of friends of the canine variety, just as some have started to do for our feline friends.

title: Universal Studios Japan partners with manga horror master Junji Ito’s Tomie
description: Undying school girl enthralls zombie horde in new artwork, and maybe elsewhere too. After generations of Tokyo Disneyland being the first thing that many people in Japan think of when they hear the words “theme park,” Osaka’s Universal Studios Japan has gained considerable ground on its rival in recent years. A lot of that is […]
content:
Undying school girl enthralls zombie horde in new artwork, and maybe elsewhere too.

After generations of Tokyo Disneyland being the first thing that many people in Japan think of when they hear the words “theme park,” Osaka’s Universal Studios Japan has gained considerable ground on its rival in recent years. A lot of that is thanks to USJ actively pursuing things that Disney can’t, such as collaborations with Japanese pop culture franchises from the anime/manga sphere or focusing on non-kid-friendly scares during Halloween season, and now the park is going to be doing both at once with a collaboration with one of the all-time masters of manga horror, Junji Ito.

Ito is a prolific creator with no shortage of works that would have been a thematic fit for a crossover with USJ’s Halloween Horror Nights event. Uzumaki and Gyo were no doubt strong candidates, but it’s the undying schoolgirl Tomie, hailing from the series of the same name, who was ultimately chosen. Tomie’s bewitching presence and powers will be put to use on a line of exclusive merchandise showing her leading a hoard of zombies through Universal Studios Japan, with Ito’s artwork gracing T-shirts, key chains, notebooks, stickers, and towels.

It’s worth pointing out that, in the announcement of the partnership, USJ makes sure to specify that the hordes of undead under Tomie’s control are “street zombies,” the costumed performers who roam the park during Halloween Horror Nights. It would seem like this would suggest that visitors might be able to encounter Tomie herself among the creatures walking the park’s grounds. There’s been no official promise of that, but it would be unusual for USJ to offer merchandise of a franchise that has no other presence at the park.

In any case, the Universal Studios Japan Junji Ito collection goes on sale September 9 inside the park, and this year’s Halloween Horror Nights festivities will be held from September 11 to November 8. And even if Tomie herself doesn’t end up taking over part of the park, if you’re looking for thrills at Halloween Horror Nights, there’s a haunted house that’s so intense it requires a consent form before you can enter.

title: Tokyo pub prohibits talking or keeping your phone out, only lets you drink in morning on weekends
description: There are a lot of hoops to jump through at Uchida, but is this 80-year-old pub worth the hassle? When the weekend rolls around, do you like meeting up with a friend and grabbing a drink or two? Hey, what a coincidence! So do we! And when you and your friends are choosing where to […]
content:
There are a lot of hoops to jump through at Uchida, but is this 80-year-old pub worth the hassle?

When the weekend rolls around, do you like meeting up with a friend and grabbing a drink or two? Hey, what a coincidence! So do we!

And when you and your friends are choosing where to knock back a couple cold ones at, do you find yourself gravitating towards places that have a long, long list of rules for customers to follow? No? How about places that require you to get up vey early in the morning and start drinking before noon? Hmm…not so crazy about that either, huh? Well, in that case the Japanese pub Uchida, in Tokyo’s Tateishi neighborhood, might not be the place for you.

To be honest, we weren’t sure whether or not Uchida would be the place for us either, but despite its strict customer conduct codes and bizarre operating hours, Uchida has been in business since 1946. You don’t last eight decades in the restaurant business by pure luck, especially in a market as competitive as Tokyo, so we figured there must be something that makes it worth it to set an early alarm and navigate Uchida’s byzantine web of etiquette expectations, so that’s what we set out to do.

Let’s start with the schedule. Even on weekdays, Uchida shuts down pretty early, closing at 7 p.m. On weekends, though, the place is only open from 10 a.m. to noon. That doesn’t mean you can just roll up at 10 and expect to get in, though. Because of Uchida’s popularity, customers start showing up to put their names in the queue for seats long before the restaurant opens. Some die-hard fans show up before 6 a.m., and when we arrived at 7, there were already more than 30 people who’d gotten there before us.

The Uchida (宇ち多゛) shutters are still closed in the early morning, but staff are stationed around the back of the restaurant to give out numbers to aspiring customers so that they don’t have to stand in line for the hours waiting to get in. You don’t get a piece of paper or text message, though. The staff simply tells you your number verbally, and it’s up to you to remember it. They’ll also tell you what time you should come back and wait outside for your number block to be called, which in our case was 9:20 a.m.

So if you’re headed to Uchida on the weekend, you’re going to have some time to kill, which is actually good, because it’ll give you time to review the many rules the restaurant has. What kind of rules? Well…

● All photography other than pictures of food/drink is prohibited.
● Placing your phone on your table or the counter is prohibited.
● Please refrain from using your phone as much as possible.
● Refrain from talking with others as much as possible.
● Do not eat with your elbows on the table/counter.
● Shoulder/backpacks must be removed and carried in the hand/in front of yourself when entering/exiting the restaurant.
● All party members must be present in line in order to be admitted (no lining up and having your friends join later).
● Dining time is limited to one hour.
● Customers who have already been drinking elsewhere will not be admitted.

Granted, that last one shouldn’t be a problem at 10 a.m., but the rest are pretty strict. Then there’s Uchida’s ordering system. Uchida’s specialty is motsu, or pork/beef organ meats, and they offer them both grilled and boiled. There’s a rigid protocol to how customers have to place their orders. If you’re ordering grilled motsu, first, you call out the cut you want…
● reba (liver)
● shiro (intestine)
● abura (fat)
● hatsu (heart)
● nankotsu (cartilage)
● teppo (rectum)
● kobukuro (uterus)
● tan (tongue)

…followed by your desired seasoning…
● tare (sauce)
● shio (salt)
● miso
● suyaki (plain)

…and finally how you want it cooked.
● futsu (standard)
● wakayaki (tender-cooked)
● yokuyaki (well-done)

If you’re ordering boiled motsu, you also start by calling out the cut you want, but next you have to say nama. Ordinarily this is the word for “raw” in Japanese, but at Uchida it’s what they call boiled motsu. Last, you pick your seasoning type, with the options this time being…
● osu (vinegar)
● shio (salt)
● amaino (sauce)
● shoyu (soy sauce)

So, for example, an order for grilled motsu could be “reba miso yokuyaki,” but not “miso reba yokuyaki.” Likewise, “nankotsu nama shio” is a valid boiled motsu order, but “nama shio nanjkotsu” is not.

▼ A plate of tan nama osu

After you enter the restaurant and are shown to your seat, the staff will ask what you’d like for your first order. This is the one and only time they’ll do that. From that point on, if you want to order anything you need to just call out what you want.

Since photos of anything other than the food and drinks are prohibited, we can’t show you much of the interior, but rest assured that it’s an old-school, down-to-earth environment, the kind of place where the ambiance comes from the weathered counter’s decades of history, rather than trendy furniture or fancy decorations. Uchida’s prices feel like a throwback too, with two-skewer orders of roast motsu or plates of boiled motsu for just 250 yen (US$1.60). A small bottle of Kirin beer is 500 yen, which is a good deal, but for half that price you can get Uchida’s flagship beverage, umewari.

This is a cocktail of Takara-brand shochu and ume (Japanese plum) syrup. It’s very strong and very sweet, and something you’re unlikely to find in other Japanese pubs. Looking around, we saw that almost every other customer ordered at least one glass of umewari during their meal.

▼ Ume syrup being added to the shochu to make umewari

But despite Uchida’s decidedly blue-collar vibe and encouragement of not just day drinking, but morning drinking, this is not a rowdy establishment. Remember, customers are asked to refrain from conversation, and the non-order chatter was at a minimum. Instead, customers were quietly focused on the drinks and food in front of them. That doesn’t that the mood is hostile or oppressive, though, and part-way through our meal, in a quiet voice, the patron seated next to us informed us “If you don’t order the kashira (head) motsu soon, it’ll sell out.” Armed with this insider information, we managed to get in an order of “kashira shiro wakayaki” while it was still available.

As further proof of Uchida’s lack of desire for booze-filled boisterousness, and of the pub’s penchant for rules, remember how we said the umewari is a strong cocktail? Uchida has a rule that first-time customers are not permitted to order more than three glasses of it, and they might even cut you off before that. When a woman seated near us tried to order a third glass, the staff authoritatively refused, telling her “Keep it at two today,” apparently concerned that the cumulative alcohol content would be more than she could handle.

▼ Shiro tare yokuyaki

Uchida has one more special drink on its menu, the 300-yen hachi budoshu, a honey-sweetened wine, which we also ordered. It was surprisingly smooth, and we drank it down very happily.

▼ The Uchida storefront during operating hours, and as much of the interior as we can show

All in all, a morning visit to Uchida makes for a uniquely special experience, one unlike any we’ve ever had before, and there was even an added bonus when it was all done. Because of how each customer’s seating time is limited to one hour, when we left the pub, so too were a number of other customers. Once again able to converse freely, everyone exchanged greetings, and after chatting for a bit, we all went out for an afternoon round at a different nearby pub.

So yes, Uchida is worth getting up early for, and also, after drinking in the morning, probably going to bed early that night too.

title: Studio Ghibli composer Jo Hisaishi just set three Guinness Records
description: Composer for My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, and Spirited Away broke two records on his trip to the U.S. By just about any measure, Joe Hisaishi has an enviable resume. The go-to composer for the soundtracks of Studio Ghibli’s anime films, especially those directed by studio co-founder Hayao Miyazaki, Hisaishi has also collaborated multiple times […]
content:
Composer for My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, and Spirited Away broke two records on his trip to the U.S.

By just about any measure, Joe Hisaishi has an enviable resume. The go-to composer for the soundtracks of Studio Ghibli’s anime films, especially those directed by studio co-founder Hayao Miyazaki, Hisaishi has also collaborated multiple times with live-action film director Takeshi Kitano/Beat Takeshi. But even after decades of success and critical acclaim, Hisaishi is still achieving new career milestones, as this summer he’s been certified as having set three Guinness Records.

The first record recognizes Hisaishi for most tickets sold by a classical composer at Tokyo Dome, based on the 133,453 people who came out to see the Studio Ghibli Film Concert Tour performances at the stadium on July 16 and 17 of last year.

Last month, Hisaishi also set the record for the most tickets sold for a classical concert run at the Hollywood Bowl. The Los Angeles venue hosted Joe Hisaishi Film Music Concert Featuring Studio Ghibli & More between July 21 and 23, with a total of 45,538 tickets.

▼ Hisaishi taking the stage at the Hollywood Bowl, where he conducted the Los Angeles Philharmonic orchestra and California State University’s Fullerton University Singers

View this post on Instagram

▼ Hisaishi’s view of the Bowl crowd

View this post on Instagram

Finally, this week Hisaishi was certified as the record-holder for the longest single-run residency by a classical composer at New York’s Radio City Music Hall, where he conducted MasterVoices and the Orchestra of St. Luke’s, as well as personally played the piano, every night from August 11 to 17.

▼ Hisaishi, who now has so many Guinness Records that he can’t hold them all at the same time

View this post on Instagram

“I am overjoyed at the honor of receiving these Guinness Records,” said Hisaishi after they were made official. “At all of the performances, the support from the audiences was incredible. I will continue working hard so that many people can enjoy coming to my concerts.”

Despite their venue-specific nature, the three achievements are still officially classified by Guinness as “World Records,” and one could make the argument that, as modern compositions, Hisaishi’s music would be more accurately described as “symphonic” or “orchestral” than “classical.” Linguistic quibbles aside, though, these are all still achievements to be proud of, and another example of how anime entertainment can help lead to broader interests in culture and the arts around the world.

Source: Universal Music Japan, Guinness World Records (1, 2, 3), Hollywood Bowl, MSG Entertainment

title: New Shinkansen Supreme Class private cabins get try-before-you-ride displays at Tokyo, other stations
description: Wondering if this extra luxury on your Japan trip is worth the extra ticket cost? Here’s a free way to find out. Japan’s fastest trains are getting an extra dash of fanciness this fall, as the Shinkansen is adding private and semi-private cabins to the connected Tokaido and Sanyo bullet train lines that stretch from […]
content:
Wondering if this extra luxury on your Japan trip is worth the extra ticket cost? Here’s a free way to find out.

Japan’s fastest trains are getting an extra dash of fanciness this fall, as the Shinkansen is adding private and semi-private cabins to the connected Tokaido and Sanyo bullet train lines that stretch from Tokyo to Fukuoka, with stops in cities such as Kyoto, Osaka, and Hiroshima along the way. Naturally, these high-class seats come at considerably higher prices than even those in the Shinkansen’s already existing premium Green Car class, so to help travelers decide whether or not they’re worth splurging on, Japan Railways/JR is installing Supreme Class mockups inside select stations so that you can try them out before taking your bullet train ride.

The Supreme Class trial mockups will appear in Tokyo, Shin Osaka, Hiroshima, and Hakata (Fukuoka) Stations in September, and then in Nagoya Station in November. All locations will allow participants to sit in the simulated Supreme Class Cabin…

…and at Tokyo and Nagoya Stations you can also try out the Supreme Class Seat, JR’s designation for the new semi-private cabin seats.

Each participant gets around 5 to 10 minutes of seat time, plus an explanation from a JR staff member about the Supreme Class amenities. At the Tokyo, Osaka, and Nagoya locations you’ll also receive a bottle of Supreme Class mineral water, and at those locations if you fill out a brief survey, each group can also take home a matcha Baumkuchen cake from renowned Kyoto green tea confectioner Tsujiri, which will also be supplying the sweets as a complimentary welcome gift to Supreme Class passengers once the Shinkansen service begins.

The complete schedule for the Supreme Class trial mockups is:
● Tokyo Station (Yaesu Chuo Gate event space): September 1-13
11 a.m.-7 p.m. (9:30 a.m.-5 p.m. September 1 only)
● Shin Osaka Station (Chuo Gate): September 15-20
11 a.m.-7 p.m.
● Hiroshima Station (North Gate 1st floor): September 22-27
11 a.m.-7 p.m.
● Hakata Station (Hakata Gate 1st floor): September 29-October 4
11 a.m.-7 p.m.
● Nagoya Station (Chuo Event Space):: November 1-8
11 a.m.-7 p.m.

Reservations can be made for Tokyo, Osaka, and Nagoya locations via the Line QR code below, though they’re not required as long as there’s space available. The Hiroshima and Fukuoka mockups are simply first-come, first-served.

Shinkansen trains with Supreme Class Cabins and Seats are scheduled to start running on October 1.

title: Pokémon and Polaroid reveal collaboration with adorable Pikachu and Eeveelution camera and film
description: Soon you’ll be able to use your Pokémon camera to take Pokémon photos, and then keep them in a Pokémon album too. The Pokémon franchise is built on the idea that there’s a lot of cool stuff in the world, and the only way to find it is to get out there and start looking. […]
content:
Soon you’ll be able to use your Pokémon camera to take Pokémon photos, and then keep them in a Pokémon album too.

The Pokémon franchise is built on the idea that there’s a lot of cool stuff in the world, and the only way to find it is to get out there and start looking. You may not know what you’re going to see on your adventures, but you can be sure there’s going to be something to remember.

That same sense of spontaneous discovery and shared memories is also the core appeal of Polaroid’s instant cameras, and that kindred spirit is now bringing them together with the reveal of a new Pokémon Polaroid collaboration.

Three special themed cameras are on the way, with the most obviously Pocket Monster-inspired being the Special Edition Go Gen 3–Pikachu model.

With that distinctive Pikachu tail strap, this one signals right away that no matter what might be in your viewfinder at the moment, you’ve always got Pikachu in your heart.

▼ And if you’re oohing and ahhing over that film frame, we’ll have more on it later in this article.

A bit more subtle is the Special Edition Now Gen 3-Pokémon design, but even from afar, fellow fans will quickly pick up on the color scheme being an homage to a Poké Ball.

Pikachu’s presence is pretty much always a given in crossovers like this, but if there’s a second specific species being represented, it’s often Eevee. Polaroid, though, is instead giving a salute to one of Eevee’s many evolutions with the Special Edition Go Gen 3-Sylveon camera.

And yes, Pokémon Polaroid film is also part of the partnership, with the three options here being the Polaroid Color i-Type Film-Pokémon Edition, Polaroid Go Color Film- Pokémon Pikachu Edition Double Pack, and Polaroid Go Color Film–Pokémon Sylveon Edition Double Pack.

The Pikachu and Sylveon versions are all about their respective Pokémon, while a variety of species appear on the frames of the Pokémon Edition film.

Included with the themed film are some cool dark slides for other members of the Pokémon’s evolutionary family trees and some, but not all, of the original starter trio..

▼ Sorry, Squirtle, but it looks like Mew took your place.

And rounding out the collection are Poké Ball-style camera cases, photo albums, and camera straps.

The Pikachu and Eevee cameras are priced at US$99.99, and the Poké Ball color-scheme camera at US$139.99, both equivalent to a US$10-premium over non-themed Go Gen 3 and Now Gen 3 models. The film packs range from US$22.99 to US$24.99, while the Poké Ball camera case and photo album are US$24.99 each and the Poké Ball-motif camera strap is US$14.99.

Preorders for the entire lineup start on August 25 through the Polaroid online store, and the company says the items will also be offered through the Pokémon Center online shop’s U.S., U.K., and Canada storefronts, with a release date of October 5.
